title: Why the sky is blue
text: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow, each with a different wavelength. Violet and blue light have the shortest wavelengths; red has the longest. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it meets countless molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, which are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. Such tiny particles scatter light in all directions, but they do not treat every colour equally: shorter wavelengths are scattered much more strongly than longer ones. This effect is called Rayleigh scattering, after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh, who worked out its mathematics in the nineteenth century. Because blue light is scattered so strongly, it reaches our eyes from every part of the sky, and the whole sky appears blue. Violet is scattered even more, so why is the sky not violet? Part of the answer is that sunlight contains less violet than blue, some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels a much longer path through the air to reach us. Along the way most of the blue is scattered out of the direct beam, so the light that remains is rich in orange and red. Larger particles, such as the water droplets in clouds, scatter all colours about equally, which is why clouds look white or grey rather than blue.

stem: According to the passage, the nitrogen and oxygen molecules that scatter sunlight are
options: much larger than the wavelength of visible light
about the same size as the droplets in clouds
far smaller than the wavelength of visible light
made mostly of water vapour from the oceans
explanation: The third sentence says the molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. Cloud droplets are described later as ‘larger particles’ that scatter all colours equally, so the molecules are not the same size as them.

options: black
blue
violet
white
explanation: The passage explains that the sky looks blue because air molecules scatter sunlight towards our eyes from every direction. With almost no atmosphere there is almost nothing to scatter light, so the sky away from the Sun would look black. Blue is tempting only if one forgets that the colour comes from the air, not from sunlight itself.

stem: The question ‘why is the sky not violet?’ is raised mainly in order to
options: show that Lord Rayleigh's mathematics was mistaken
suggest that the sky is in fact slightly violet
explain why clouds appear white rather than blue
address a puzzle the explanation seems to raise
explanation: Since the passage has just said that violet is scattered even more than blue, a reader might expect a violet sky; the next sentence gives three reasons why it is not. Nothing in the passage says Rayleigh's mathematics was wrong, and clouds are explained separately at the end.

title: A measure for everyone
text: For most of history, units of measurement varied from place to place. A foot or a pound in one town might differ from the foot or pound in the next, and traders, builders and scientists constantly had to convert between local standards. In the 1790s, scientists in France set out to design a system that would be the same for everyone and based on nature rather than on custom. They defined the metre as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along a line passing through Paris, and two surveyors spent several years measuring part of that distance. Units of volume and mass were linked to the metre: a litre was the volume of a cube one-tenth of a metre on each side, and a kilogram was close to the mass of a litre of water. Above all, larger and smaller units were related by powers of ten, so converting kilometres to metres needed only a shift of the decimal point. The new system was slow to win acceptance, even in France, because people were attached to familiar units. Over the following two centuries, however, it spread across the world and became the basis of the International System of Units used in science today. Its definitions have since been refined: the metre is now fixed by the speed of light, which can be measured far more precisely than the size of the Earth.

stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: the work of two French surveyors in the eighteenth century
how a shared system of measurement arose and spread
the reasons why traders resisted all new units
the methods used to measure the speed of light
explanation: The passage moves from the confusion of local units to the French design of the metre, litre and kilogram, then to its slow acceptance and worldwide spread. The surveyors are one detail in that story, and the speed of light appears only in the final sentence.

stem: In the passage, the word ‘refined’ most nearly means
options: made more polite
purified chemically
made more precise
made more costly
explanation: The sentence explains that the metre is now fixed by the speed of light, which can be measured ‘far more precisely’ than the Earth, so the definitions have been made more exact. ‘Purified’ is a meaning of refined used for sugar or oil, not for definitions.

stem: According to the passage, the metre is now defined using the speed of light because
options: it can be measured more accurately than the Earth
the size of the Earth had changed since the 1790s
the original survey was found to have no errors
people in France still preferred their familiar old units
explanation: The last sentence says the speed of light can be measured far more precisely than the size of the Earth. The passage never claims that the Earth itself changed, and French attachment to old units explains the system's slow start, not its later redefinition.

title: Why ice floats
text: Most substances shrink as they cool and are densest in their solid form, so a solid piece usually sinks in its own liquid. Water is a striking exception. As water cools, it becomes denser only until it reaches about 4 °C; below that temperature it begins to expand again, and when it freezes it expands by roughly nine per cent. Ice is therefore less dense than liquid water, and it floats. The explanation lies in hydrogen bonding. In liquid water, molecules are constantly forming and breaking weak bonds with their neighbours, which lets them pack fairly closely. In ice, each molecule is held by hydrogen bonds to four others in a fixed, open pattern that contains a great deal of empty space. This odd behaviour has large consequences. In winter, the surface of a lake cools first. Water at 4 °C sinks to the bottom, and the colder water stays on top, where it eventually freezes. The layer of ice then acts like a lid, insulating the water below, so that lakes in cold regions freeze from the top down and seldom freeze solid. Fish and other creatures can survive the winter in the liquid water beneath. The same expansion causes trouble for people: water that freezes inside a pipe or a crack in a rock can split it open, which is why water pipes in cold places are buried or wrapped.

stem: According to the passage, ice floats on water because
options: ice is less dense than liquid water
ice contains trapped bubbles of air
cold water always rises to the top
ice molecules are heavier than water
explanation: The passage says water expands by about nine per cent when it freezes, so ‘Ice is therefore less dense than liquid water, and it floats.’ The empty space in ice comes from the open pattern of hydrogen bonds, not from trapped air bubbles.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘open’ in ‘a fixed, open pattern’ most nearly means
options: honest and frank
ready for business
not yet decided
having gaps or spaces
explanation: The phrase is explained at once: the pattern ‘contains a great deal of empty space’, so open means full of gaps. ‘Honest and frank’ is the sense used for people, not for the arrangement of molecules.

stem: It can be inferred that if ice were denser than liquid water, lakes in cold regions would most likely
options: never freeze at all
freeze from the bottom up
stay at exactly 4 °C
freeze faster at the surface
explanation: Lakes freeze from the top down only because the floating ice forms a lid. If ice were denser, it would sink as it formed and collect on the bottom, so a lake would fill with ice from below. The passage gives no reason to think the water would stop freezing altogether.

title: Summer on the Deosai plateau
text: Deosai, in Gilgit-Baltistan, is one of the highest plateaus in the world, a rolling plain that lies at an average height of roughly 4,000 metres above sea level. For more than half the year it is buried under deep snow and almost no one goes there. When the snow melts in early summer, the plateau changes completely: streams fill with clear meltwater, and the grassland is covered with wild flowers that bloom quickly during the short growing season. The plateau was declared a national park in 1993, largely to protect the Himalayan brown bear, whose numbers had fallen very low because of hunting and disturbance. Brown bears spend the long winter in dens, living on fat stored during summer, when they feed on grasses, roots and small mammals such as marmots. Golden marmots are themselves among the most noticeable animals on Deosai, whistling a warning from the entrances of their burrows when a person or predator approaches. Since the park was created, regular monitoring has recorded a gradual rise in bear numbers. The plateau's growing popularity with summer visitors brings its own pressures, however. Jeeps that leave the tracks can damage the thin soil, which recovers only slowly in such a cold climate, and litter left near the lakes may draw bears towards people. Careful management of tourism is therefore now seen as part of protecting the park.

stem: According to the passage, Deosai was declared a national park mainly to
options: control the number of golden marmots
build better jeep tracks for visitors
study the plateau's summer wild flowers
protect the Himalayan brown bear
explanation: The passage says the plateau became a national park in 1993 ‘largely to protect the Himalayan brown bear’, whose numbers had fallen very low. Marmots are mentioned as bear food and as noticeable animals, not as the reason for the park.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘pressures’ most nearly means
options: physical forces on the ground
harmful demands or strains
weather systems bringing snow
urgent deadlines for park staff
explanation: The sentence about ‘pressures’ is followed by examples of harm from visitors: jeeps damaging soil and litter drawing bears towards people. ‘Physical forces on the ground’ is tempting because of the jeeps, but litter is not a physical force, so the word means strains or burdens in general.

stem: It can be inferred that damage to Deosai's soil by vehicles is a particular concern because
options: bears dig up the soil when searching for roots
the flowers there bloom only every few years
the cold climate makes recovery very slow
the soil is too rich to support grassland
explanation: The passage says the thin soil ‘recovers only slowly in such a cold climate’, so tyre damage lasts a long time. The flowers are said to bloom quickly each short summer, not every few years, and bears eating roots is never linked to soil damage.

title: The rule of 72
text: When money is saved or invested at compound interest, the interest earned each year is added to the total, and the following year's interest is calculated on that larger amount. Growth of this kind speeds up over time, and it can be hard to judge in one's head how quickly a sum will grow. Bankers and economists therefore use a simple shortcut known as the rule of 72. To estimate how many years it takes for an amount to double, divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate of growth. At 6 per cent a year, savings double in about 12 years; at 9 per cent, in about 8 years. The rule is only an approximation, but for rates between about 2 and 15 per cent it is usually accurate to within a year. The number 72 is chosen partly because it divides neatly by many small whole numbers, such as 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, which makes mental arithmetic easy. The same shortcut works for anything that grows at a steady percentage rate. If a town's population rises by 3 per cent a year, it will double in about 24 years. It also works for prices: if prices rise by 8 per cent a year, money loses half its buying power in roughly 9 years. The rule cannot predict what future rates will be, but it turns an abstract percentage into a period of time that people can picture.

stem: According to the passage, at a growth rate of 9 per cent a year, an amount doubles in about
options: 6 years
8 years
9 years
12 years
explanation: The passage states that at 9 per cent a sum doubles in about 8 years, which is 72 ÷ 9. Twelve years is the figure given for 6 per cent, and 9 years is the figure for prices rising at 8 per cent.

stem: The author mentions that 72 divides neatly by many small whole numbers in order to
options: show that the rule is exact for every rate of growth
prove that interest rates are always whole numbers
suggest that bankers dislike doing mental arithmetic
explain why 72 is a convenient number for the rule
explanation: The sentence says 72 is chosen partly because it divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, ‘which makes mental arithmetic easy’. The passage calls the rule ‘only an approximation’, so it cannot be showing that the rule is exact.

stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Savings at 4 per cent a year would take about 18 years to double.
The rule of 72 gives exact answers for rates above 15 per cent.
A population growing by 3 per cent a year doubles in 12 years.
Prices rising by 8 per cent a year double roughly every 72 years.
explanation: Applying the rule as the passage describes, 72 ÷ 4 = 18 years. The passage gives 24 years, not 12, for a population growing at 3 per cent, and it says the rule is reliable only between about 2 and 15 per cent, never exact above that.

title: How a refrigerator moves heat
text: A refrigerator does not create cold. It works by moving heat out of its insides and releasing it into the kitchen, and it does this with a fluid called a refrigerant that is pumped round a closed loop of pipes. The key to the process is that a liquid absorbs heat when it evaporates, which is why wet skin feels cool in a breeze. Inside the fridge, the refrigerant flows through coils as a cold liquid at low pressure. It boils easily, and as it turns into vapour it takes heat from the food and the air around it. The vapour then passes to a compressor, a pump driven by an electric motor, which squeezes it into a smaller volume. Compression makes the vapour hot, hotter than the room, so when it flows through the coils at the back or bottom of the fridge, it gives up its heat to the kitchen air and condenses into a liquid again. Finally, the liquid passes through a narrow opening into a region of low pressure, where it cools sharply and is ready to begin the cycle once more. Because the heat removed from the food ends up in the room, together with the heat produced by the motor, leaving the fridge door open on a hot day actually makes a kitchen warmer, not cooler. For the same reason, a fridge works best with space around its back coils, so that the heat can escape.

stem: According to the passage, the refrigerant takes heat from the food when it
options: is squeezed by the compressor
condenses in the back coils
evaporates inside the fridge
is pumped out into the kitchen
explanation: The passage says the refrigerant flows inside the fridge as a cold liquid and, ‘as it turns into vapour’, takes heat from the food. Condensing in the back coils is the step where it gives heat out to the kitchen, the reverse of what the question asks.

stem: The example of wet skin feeling cool in a breeze is included in order to
options: illustrate that evaporation absorbs heat
show that fridges should stand in breezy rooms
explain why the compressor becomes hot
suggest that people should wet their skin on hot days
explanation: The example follows the statement that a liquid absorbs heat when it evaporates, the principle on which the fridge works. The compressor's heat is explained later by compression, not by evaporation.

stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: The coils at the back of a fridge should be kept fully covered.
A fridge pressed tightly against a wall would likely work less well.
The compressor is the coldest part of the whole refrigerator.
Refrigerant escapes from the closed pipes each time it turns into vapour.
explanation: The last sentence says a fridge works best with space around its back coils so that heat can escape; pressing it against a wall removes that space. Covering the coils would also trap heat, and the refrigerant moves round a closed loop, so it does not escape.

title: Reading the Rosetta Stone
text: For more than a thousand years, no one could read the hieroglyphs carved on the temples and tombs of ancient Egypt. The knowledge had been lost, and many scholars believed the signs were purely symbolic pictures that stood for ideas rather than sounds. The breakthrough came from a slab of dark stone found in 1799 near the town of Rashid, known in English as Rosetta, in the Nile Delta. The stone carried the same official decree written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic, a later everyday Egyptian script, and in ancient Greek, which scholars could still read. The Greek text acted as a key. The English scientist Thomas Young made early progress, showing that some signs enclosed in oval rings, called cartouches, spelled the names of rulers such as Ptolemy. The French scholar Jean-François Champollion went much further. He knew Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language, and used it to work out the sounds of many signs. In 1822 he announced that hieroglyphic writing mixed signs that stand for sounds with signs that stand for whole words or ideas, which is why earlier attempts that treated every sign as a picture had failed. His work opened thousands of inscriptions to study, and with them much of the history of ancient Egypt. The Rosetta Stone itself is now kept in the British Museum in London.

stem: According to the passage, the Greek text on the Rosetta Stone was important because
options: it was the oldest of the three scripts
it named every ruler of ancient Egypt
it was written in a later everyday script
scholars of the time could still read it
explanation: The passage says the decree appeared in ancient Greek, ‘which scholars could still read’, and so the Greek ‘acted as a key’ to the other two versions. The later everyday script was Demotic, not Greek.

stem: According to the passage, earlier attempts to read hieroglyphs failed mainly because scholars
options: had no surviving examples of hieroglyphic writing
could not read any ancient Greek texts
treated every sign as a picture of an idea
refused to look at the Rosetta Stone
explanation: Champollion showed that the script mixed sound signs with word signs, ‘which is why earlier attempts that treated every sign as a picture had failed’. Hieroglyphs were carved on many temples and tombs, so a lack of examples was not the problem.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘key’ most nearly means
options: a metal tool for opening locks
a means of solving a problem
the most important person
a set of notes in music
explanation: The Greek text ‘acted as a key’ because scholars could read it and use it to work out the meaning of the other two scripts, so it was a means of unlocking a puzzle. The literal metal tool is the everyday sense, which does not fit a written text.

title: The clever octopus
text: The octopus is a mollusc, a relative of snails and clams, yet it behaves in ways that seem surprisingly clever. In aquariums, octopuses have learned to unscrew the lids of jars to reach food inside, and some have escaped from their tanks by squeezing through tiny gaps, since their bodies contain no bones and their only hard part is a beak. In the wild, certain species collect halves of coconut shells and carry them about to use as shelters. Their nervous system is organised very differently from ours. An octopus has roughly 500 million nerve cells, but about two-thirds of them are located in its eight arms rather than in its central brain. Each arm can therefore touch, taste and respond to its surroundings with a degree of independence, so the brain does not need to direct every movement. The animal is also a master of disguise. Special cells in its skin allow it to change colour and pattern in a fraction of a second, matching rocks, sand or seaweed, and some species can even change the texture of their skin. Other unusual features include three hearts and blue blood, which carries oxygen using a copper-based compound instead of the iron-based haemoglobin found in human blood. Despite all this ability, most octopuses live only one or two years, so whatever they know must be learned quickly and largely without help from parents.

options: central brain

skin

explanation: The passage states that about two-thirds of the roughly 500 million nerve cells are located in the eight arms ‘rather than in its central brain’. This is why each arm can act with some independence.

stem: In the passage, the phrase ‘a master of disguise’ refers to the octopus's ability to
options: escape from tanks through tiny gaps
change its colour and pattern
unscrew the lids of jars for food
survive without any bones
explanation: The sentence that follows the phrase explains it: special skin cells let the octopus change colour and pattern in a fraction of a second to match rocks, sand or seaweed. Escaping through gaps shows flexibility, not disguise.

stem: The final sentence suggests that the octopus's abilities are especially remarkable because it
options: must acquire them quickly and mostly alone
learns most of its skills from older octopuses
lives far longer than most other molluscs
uses its central brain to control every arm
explanation: The last sentence says most octopuses live only one or two years, so what they know must be learned quickly and largely without help from parents. That rules out learning from older octopuses, and the passage says the brain does not need to direct every movement.

title: Counting the seconds to thunder
text: Lightning and thunder are produced by the same event, yet we usually see the flash before we hear the rumble. The reason is the great difference in the speeds of light and sound. Light travels so fast that the flash reaches an observer almost instantly, while sound in air covers only about 340 metres each second. Counting the seconds between flash and thunder therefore gives a rough measure of distance: a gap of three seconds means the lightning struck about one kilometre away. Thunder itself is the sound of air being heated suddenly. A lightning channel is only a few centimetres wide, but within a tiny fraction of a second it heats the air to tens of thousands of degrees, several times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air expands so violently that it sends out a shock wave, which we hear as a sharp crack nearby or as a long rumble farther away. The rumbling happens because a lightning channel is several kilometres long, so sound from different parts of it arrives at slightly different times and also echoes off hills and buildings. Safety advice follows from these facts. If thunder can be heard, the storm is close enough for lightning to reach you, because strikes can occur many kilometres from the centre of a storm. People are therefore advised to go indoors when they first hear thunder and to stay there until it has stopped for some time.

stem: Based on the passage, a gap of six seconds between a flash and its thunder means the lightning struck about
options: half a kilometre away
one kilometre away
two kilometres away
six kilometres away
explanation: The passage says a three-second gap means about one kilometre, so six seconds means about two kilometres (sound travels about 340 m each second, and 6 × 340 ≈ 2,000 m). ‘Six kilometres’ wrongly treats each second as a kilometre.

stem: According to the passage, distant thunder sounds like a long rumble rather than a single crack because
options: light from the flash always reaches the observer well before the sound
the air in the channel is cooler than the surface of the Sun
the lightning channel is only a few centimetres wide
sound from different parts of the channel arrives at different times
explanation: The passage explains that the channel is several kilometres long, so sound from its different parts arrives at slightly different times and echoes off hills and buildings. The flash arriving first explains the delay before thunder, not its rumbling, and the air is described as hotter, not cooler, than the Sun's surface.

stem: The final three sentences of the passage mainly serve to
options: show how the facts described lead to practical safety advice
describe a new and more accurate method of measuring lightning heat
argue that storms are less dangerous than most people believe
explain why lightning never strikes the same place twice
explanation: The sentence ‘Safety advice follows from these facts’ introduces the advice to go indoors when thunder is first heard, because strikes can occur far from a storm's centre. The passage stresses danger rather than playing it down, so the third option is the reverse of its point.

title: The pull of the first number
text: Imagine two groups of shoppers asked to guess the price of a second-hand bicycle. Before guessing, the first group is asked whether the bicycle is worth more or less than 30,000 rupees; the second group is asked the same question with a figure of 8,000 rupees. In experiments of this kind, the first group usually gives much higher estimates than the second, even though both groups see the same bicycle and know that the opening figure is merely a starting point. Psychologists call this tendency anchoring: an initial number, once heard, pulls later judgements towards itself. The effect was described in the 1970s by the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, who found that even a number produced by spinning a wheel could influence people's estimates of unrelated quantities. Anchoring appears in many everyday settings. A shopkeeper who first shows a very expensive model makes the next one seem reasonable; a seller who opens a negotiation with a high price often ends with a higher agreed price than one who opens low. Experts are not immune, although knowledge of a subject can reduce the effect. One way to resist anchoring is to form your own estimate before hearing anyone else's figure; another is to consider deliberately why the anchor might be wrong. Neither method removes the influence entirely, but both make it weaker.

stem: According to the passage, the experiment with a spinning wheel showed that
options: experts are never influenced by anchors
people ignore numbers that they know to be clearly unrelated
shoppers always guess second-hand prices accurately
even a random number could affect people's estimates
explanation: Tversky and Kahneman found that ‘even a number produced by spinning a wheel’ could influence estimates of unrelated quantities. That is the opposite of people ignoring unrelated numbers, and the passage says experts are ‘not immune’.

stem: In the passage, the word ‘immune’ most nearly means
options: protected from disease
unaffected
opposed
unaware
explanation: ‘Experts are not immune, although knowledge of a subject can reduce the effect’ means experts are still affected by anchors. ‘Protected from disease’ is the medical sense of the word, which does not fit a discussion of judgement.

stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates anchoring as described in the passage?
options: Usman buys a particular phone mainly because a close friend recommends it.
Fatima buys a cheaper bag because her budget this month is limited.
Zainab offers more for a car after the seller names a high price first.
Hamza returns a new shirt to the shop after finding it does not fit.
explanation: Anchoring is an initial number pulling later judgements towards it, as when a seller who opens high ends with a higher agreed price. Zainab's offer is pulled up by the seller's first figure. Usman is swayed by advice, not by a number, so his case is not anchoring.

title: The camel's secret
text: The dromedary, or one-humped camel, is found across the dry lands of North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, including the Thar and Cholistan deserts of Pakistan. A common belief is that its hump is a store of water. In fact, the hump is mostly fat. Keeping fat in one place, rather than spread under the skin, lets heat escape more easily from the rest of the body, and the fat can be broken down for energy when food is scarce. The camel's real skill with water lies elsewhere. Its kidneys produce very concentrated urine, and its dung is so dry that it contains little water. Moisture in its breath is partly recaptured inside its nose rather than lost to the air. A camel can also allow its body temperature to rise by several degrees during the day and fall again at night, so it does not need to sweat until it is very hot. Together these features let it survive the loss of a quarter or more of its body's water, an amount that would kill most mammals. Its red blood cells are oval rather than round, which helps them keep flowing when the blood thickens and resist bursting when the animal finally drinks. And drink it does: a thirsty camel can take in more than 100 litres of water in a few minutes.

options: water

fat
explanation: The passage corrects the common belief directly: ‘In fact, the hump is mostly fat.’ Water is the popular mistake the passage sets out to correct.

explanation: These details follow the sentence ‘The camel's real skill with water lies elsewhere’: concentrated urine, dry dung and moisture recaptured in the nose all save water. None of them is linked to the hump, which the passage says is fat.

explanation: The passage says that because its temperature can rise, the camel ‘does not need to sweat until it is very hot’, and this is listed among the features that help it survive water loss. So it saves water; the first option states the opposite.

title: The square that changed scanning
text: In 1994, an engineer named Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave, part of a Japanese group that made car components, faced a practical problem. Workers tracked parts using ordinary barcodes, which store information only in a single row of lines, so several barcodes often had to be scanned for one item. Hara's team designed a square code that stores data both across and down, which allows it to hold far more information in the same space. They called it the QR code, short for ‘quick response’. Three large squares sit in three of its corners. Wherever the code is placed, these squares tell a scanner which way up it is, so it can be read from any angle and at high speed. The pattern also contains extra, repeated information, so that a code which is partly dirty or torn can often still be read correctly. Denso Wave held a patent on the design but chose not to charge others for using it, a decision that helped the code spread far beyond car factories. The real turning point came when mobile phones gained cameras able to read codes directly. Today QR codes appear on restaurant menus, product labels, tickets and shop counters, where customers scan them to pay. Their convenience has one drawback: a code reveals nothing to the eye, so a fake sticker placed over a real one can send an unwary user to a harmful website.

stem: According to the passage, the QR code was first designed to
options: make payments at shop counters
track parts used in making cars
print menus for restaurants
sell mobile phones with cameras
explanation: The passage opens with Denso Wave's workers, who tracked car parts with barcodes that needed several scans per item; the QR code was designed to solve that problem. Payments and menus are later uses that came after phones gained cameras.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘unwary’ most nearly means
options: unwilling to help
poorly educated
unlucky
not alert to danger
explanation: The sentence warns that a fake sticker can send a user to a harmful website, and an unwary user is one who does not suspect this trick. ‘Unlucky’ is tempting, but the word describes the user's lack of caution, not chance.

stem: According to the passage, the three large corner squares allow a QR code to
options: be read from any angle
store data across and down
survive being torn or dirty
be used without paying a fee
explanation: The passage says the corner squares tell a scanner which way up the code is, ‘so it can be read from any angle and at high speed’. Reading a torn or dirty code depends on the extra, repeated information, not on the squares.

title: Why onions bring tears
text: Cutting an onion is one of the few kitchen tasks that regularly brings people to tears, and the cause is a chemical defence. An intact onion contains sulfur compounds and an enzyme that acts on them, but the two are kept apart in different parts of its cells. When a knife breaks the cells open, they mix. A rapid series of reactions follows, and within about thirty seconds the onion releases a gas with the long name syn-propanethial-S-oxide. The gas drifts upwards and reaches the eyes, where it stimulates nerves in the surface of the eye. The brain responds by producing tears to wash the irritant away. For the plant, this system is useful: an animal that bites into an onion bulb receives an unpleasant surprise and may well leave the rest alone. For cooks, a few simple measures help. Chilling an onion before cutting slows the reactions and makes the gas less volatile. A very sharp knife crushes fewer cells than a blunt one, so less of the enzyme and sulfur compounds meet. Working beside an open window or under a kitchen fan carries the gas away from the face. Cooking, finally, destroys the enzyme, which is why fried or boiled onions never sting the eyes. Plant breeders have also developed onion varieties that produce much less of the gas.

stem: According to the passage, an uncut onion does not release the irritating gas because
options: it contains no sulfur compounds at all
the gas is produced only when the onion is cooked
the enzyme and sulfur compounds are kept apart
the onion skin traps all of the gas inside
explanation: The second sentence says the sulfur compounds and the enzyme ‘are kept apart in different parts of its cells’ until a knife breaks the cells. Cooking actually destroys the enzyme, so the gas is not made by cooking.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘volatile’ most nearly means
options: likely to change suddenly in mood
quick to turn into a vapour
dangerous and explosive
rare and valuable
explanation: Chilling makes the gas ‘less volatile’, meaning it escapes into the air less readily, so less reaches the eyes. The mood sense of volatile describes people, not chemicals.

stem: Based on the passage, which of the following would most likely cause the most tears?
options: Slowly cutting a room-temperature onion with a blunt knife
Cutting a chilled onion with a sharp knife beside an open window
Eating a large plate of onions that have been fried
Slicing a boiled onion under a working kitchen fan
explanation: The passage gives three ways to reduce tears: chilling, a sharp knife and moving air. The first option avoids all three, and a blunt knife crushes more cells. Cooked onions never sting because cooking destroys the enzyme, which rules out the last two options.

title: The swing that kept time
text: For most of history, mechanical clocks were poor timekeepers, often gaining or losing a quarter of an hour in a single day. The change came from a simple observation. In the late sixteenth century, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei noticed that a pendulum takes almost the same time for each swing whether it swings widely or only a little, as long as the swings are small. Later work showed that the time of a swing depends on the pendulum's length, not on the weight of the bob at its end. A longer pendulum swings more slowly: to double the time of each swing, the length must be made four times as great. Galileo did not build a working pendulum clock, but in 1656 the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens did. His clocks used the steady swing of a pendulum to control the rate at which the gears turned, and the best of them were accurate to within about fifteen seconds a day. Further improvements followed. One stubborn problem was temperature: a metal rod expands slightly in warm weather and contracts in cold. Clockmakers solved it with pendulums built from two different metals arranged so that their changes in length cancelled out. For almost three hundred years afterwards, until quartz and atomic clocks appeared in the twentieth century, the pendulum clock remained the most accurate way of keeping time.

stem: According to the passage, the time of a pendulum's swing depends mainly on its
options: length
weight
colour
width of swing
explanation: The passage states that the time of a swing ‘depends on the pendulum's length, not on the weight of the bob’. Width of swing is tempting, but Galileo's observation was that small swings take almost the same time whether wide or narrow.

stem: The passage suggests that temperature was a ‘stubborn problem’ for pendulum clocks because
options: cold weather made the gears freeze solid
warm air slowed the swinging bob through extra friction
changes in temperature altered the rod's length
heat made the clock's bob much heavier
explanation: The passage explains that a metal rod expands in warm weather and contracts in cold, and since timing depends on length, the clock's rate changed. The solution, two metals whose changes in length cancel, confirms that length was the issue, not friction.

stem: Based on the passage, a pendulum clock with an uncorrected metal rod would most likely
options: run fast in hot weather
run slow in hot weather
stop completely in cold weather
keep perfect time all year
explanation: In hot weather the rod expands, and the passage says a longer pendulum swings more slowly, so each swing takes longer and the clock falls behind. ‘Run fast in hot weather’ reverses the link between length and swing time.

title: Catching water from fog
text: Some of the driest places on Earth are not short of water in the air. Along parts of the coast of Chile and Peru, and in the mountains of southern Morocco, thick fog rolls in from the ocean on many days of the year, yet almost no rain falls. Fog harvesting aims to capture this moisture. The method is simple: a large net of fine plastic mesh, stretched between two poles, is set up facing the wind on a hillside. As fog drifts through, tiny droplets strike the threads and stick to them. Many droplets merge into larger drops, which become heavy enough to run down the mesh into a gutter at the bottom and then through a pipe to a storage tank. A single square metre of net may collect a few litres on a good day, so villages use many nets together. The idea was partly inspired by a beetle of the Namib Desert that collects fog droplets on its back and lets them roll towards its mouth. Fog nets need no fuel or electricity and are cheap to maintain, but they work only where fog is frequent and the wind blows steadily in the right direction. They are therefore not a general answer to water shortage; rather, they are a useful source for particular communities that live in the right places.

stem: According to the passage, drops of water reach the storage tank after they
options: are heated by the sun on the poles
run down the mesh into a gutter
are pumped up from the ground
fall as rain onto the hillside
explanation: The passage says merged drops become heavy enough to run down the mesh into a gutter and then through a pipe to the tank. The nets need no electricity, so no pumping is involved, and almost no rain falls in these places.

stem: The beetle of the Namib Desert is mentioned in order to
options: show that fog nets harm desert wildlife
explain why fog forms over the ocean
prove that the nets work without wind
point to a natural model for the idea
explanation: The passage says the idea ‘was partly inspired by’ the beetle, which collects fog droplets on its back. Nothing suggests harm to wildlife, and the passage states that the nets need steady wind.

stem: The author's attitude towards fog harvesting is best described as
options: strongly critical, since the nets rarely collect water
wildly enthusiastic, calling it a cure for all droughts
balanced, noting both its strengths and its limits
indifferent, giving no view on its usefulness
explanation: The author praises the nets as needing no fuel and being cheap to maintain, but adds that they work only with frequent fog and steady wind and are ‘not a general answer’. That mix of praise and limits is balanced, not wholly critical or enthusiastic.

title: From peels to soil
text: A large share of the rubbish thrown away by a typical Pakistani household, often around half, is food and garden waste: vegetable peels, tea leaves, eggshells, fallen leaves and grass cuttings. When this material is buried in a landfill site, it is squeezed together with plastic and other waste, cut off from air, and slowly broken down by microbes that do not need oxygen. That process releases methane, a gas that traps far more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide does. Composting offers a better route. In a compost heap or bin, the same waste is broken down by microbes that do need oxygen, helped by worms, insects and fungi. A good heap mixes ‘green’ materials, which are moist and rich in nitrogen, such as peels and fresh grass, with ‘brown’ materials, which are dry and rich in carbon, such as dead leaves, straw and torn cardboard. It should be kept about as damp as a squeezed sponge and turned every week or two to let in air. If it smells bad, it is usually too wet or has too much green material, and adding browns and turning it solves the problem. As the microbes work, the centre of the heap becomes warm. After two to six months, the waste becomes a dark, crumbly material that smells of soil. Mixed into a garden or into pots, it improves the soil's structure, helps it hold water and returns nutrients to plants.

stem: According to the passage, waste buried in a landfill releases methane because it
options: is mixed with too many brown materials
is broken down without oxygen
is turned too often by workers
is too dry for microbes to act
explanation: The passage says landfill waste is cut off from air and broken down by microbes that do not need oxygen, and ‘That process releases methane’. Brown materials are part of good composting, not the cause of landfill methane.

stem: According to the passage, a compost heap that smells bad should be
options: given more fresh grass and peels
covered tightly to keep out air
soaked with water every day
given more browns and turned
explanation: A bad smell means the heap is too wet or has too much green material, and ‘adding browns and turning it solves the problem’. Fresh grass and peels are green materials, so adding them would make the smell worse.

stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Composting food scraps can cut the methane that landfills release.
Compost heaps generally give off more methane than landfill sites.
Microbes in compost heaps work best when they are cut off from air.
Torn cardboard should never be added to a compost heap at all.
explanation: Landfill methane comes from waste broken down without oxygen, while composting uses microbes that need oxygen and is called ‘a better route’; so diverting scraps to compost reduces that methane. The passage says heaps should be turned to let in air, which rules out the third option.

title: Why honey keeps
text: Archaeologists excavating ancient Egyptian tombs are reported to have found pots of honey that were thousands of years old and still showed no sign of rotting. Few natural foods keep so well, and the reasons lie in honey's chemistry. Bees make honey from nectar, a thin, sugary liquid. In the hive they add an enzyme to it and fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates, leaving a thick syrup that is about four-fifths sugar and less than a fifth water. Bacteria and moulds need water to grow, and honey contains so much sugar that it draws water out of any microbe that lands in it, leaving the microbe unable to multiply. Honey is also fairly acidic, which makes it even harder for most microbes to survive. In addition, the enzyme the bees add slowly produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a substance that kills many germs. These defences work only while honey stays thick. If it absorbs water, for example when it is stored in an open jar in a damp kitchen or when a wet spoon is dipped into it, yeasts can begin to ferment it. Honey that turns grainy or solid has not spoiled; it has simply crystallised, as the sugar comes out of solution, and gentle warming will make it runny again. Honey should not be given to babies under one year old, because it can carry bacterial spores that a baby's gut cannot yet resist.

stem: According to the passage, bees turn nectar into honey mainly by
options: adding hydrogen peroxide to it
mixing it with water from the hive
removing most of its water
storing it in sealed clay pots
explanation: The passage says bees fan the nectar with their wings ‘until most of the water evaporates’, leaving a thick syrup. Hydrogen peroxide is produced slowly by the enzyme later; the bees do not add it directly.

stem: The passage suggests that dipping a wet spoon into a jar of honey is unwise because it
options: adds water that lets yeasts begin to ferment it
causes the honey to crystallise into hard, solid grains
removes the enzyme added by the bees
turns the honey too acidic to eat
explanation: Honey's defences work only while it stays thick, and a wet spoon is given as an example of how it can absorb water so that ‘yeasts can begin to ferment it’. Crystallising is described as harmless and is caused by sugar leaving solution, not by a wet spoon.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘defences’ refers to
options: the walls and wax of the beehive
the stings carried by worker bees
the warnings printed on honey jars
the features that stop microbes
explanation: ‘These defences’ sums up the three features just described: high sugar that draws water from microbes, acidity and hydrogen peroxide. Stings are a bee's defence, but the passage never mentions them.

title: The pull of the Moon
text: Twice a day, on most coasts, the sea slowly rises up the shore and then falls back. These tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity. The Moon pulls on the whole Earth, but its pull is strongest on the side of the Earth that faces it and weakest on the far side. As a result, the ocean on the near side is drawn towards the Moon, forming a bulge, and a second bulge forms on the far side, where the water is pulled less strongly than the solid Earth and is in effect left behind. As the Earth turns, a given coast passes through both bulges, which is why most places have two high tides and two low tides in a little more than a day. The Sun also raises tides, though its effect is a little less than half that of the Moon, because it is so much farther away. When the Sun, Moon and Earth lie in a line, at new moon and full moon, their effects combine to produce spring tides, with especially high high tides and low low tides. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, at the quarter moons, the tides are weaker and are called neap tides. Despite the name, spring tides have nothing to do with the season; they occur about twice every month throughout the year. The shape of the coast also matters: in narrow bays the tidal range can be many metres, while in some enclosed seas it is very small.

stem: According to the passage, the main cause of tides is
options: the gravity of the Moon
the heat of the Sun
the shape of the coast
the change of seasons
explanation: The second sentence states that tides ‘are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity’. The Sun's effect is a little less than half the Moon's, and the shape of the coast only changes the size of the tides.

stem: According to the passage, spring tides occur when
options: the season of spring begins
the Sun and Moon pull at right angles
the Sun, Moon and Earth lie in a line
the Moon is farthest from the Earth
explanation: The passage says that when the Sun, Moon and Earth lie in a line, at new and full moon, their effects combine to give spring tides. A right-angle pull at the quarter moons produces the weaker neap tides instead.

stem: The author's remark that spring tides ‘have nothing to do with the season’ is most likely included to
options: show that tides are unaffected by the Sun
correct a misunderstanding caused by the name
explain why neap tides occur at quarter moons
suggest that tides are strongest in spring
explanation: The remark begins ‘Despite the name’, showing that the author expects readers to link spring tides with the spring season and wants to correct this; they occur about twice every month. The passage says the Sun does raise tides, so the first option is wrong.

title: A theory that takes a risk
text: How can we tell a scientific theory from a claim that only sounds scientific? In the twentieth century, the philosopher Karl Popper offered an influential answer. A theory is scientific, he argued, only if it is falsifiable: it must forbid certain things from happening, so that an observation could in principle show it to be false. Consider the statement ‘all swans are white’. No number of white swans can prove it, since the next swan might be black, but a single black swan would disprove it. For Popper, this imbalance was the key to science. Scientists should not hunt for observations that agree with their theories, which are easy to find, but should design tests that could prove them wrong. A theory that survives many serious attempts at refutation earns our confidence, though never final certainty. By contrast, a claim that can be made to fit any possible outcome tells us nothing. A fortune-teller who predicts that ‘something important will happen to you soon’ can never be shown wrong, and that is exactly the weakness of the prediction. Popper's view has been criticised. Real scientists do not abandon a well-supported theory the moment one result disagrees with it; they first check the equipment, repeat the experiment and consider other explanations. Even so, his central idea remains widely taught: a good theory takes a risk by saying clearly what should not happen.

stem: According to the passage, Popper believed a theory is scientific only if it
options: has been proved true by many observations
agrees with every possible outcome
is accepted by most working scientists
could in principle be shown to be false
explanation: The passage says a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable, ‘so that an observation could in principle show it to be false’. The swan example shows why many agreeing observations cannot prove a theory true.

stem: The fortune-teller's prediction is mentioned as an example of a claim that
options: has been tested and shown to be false
cannot be proved wrong by any outcome
takes a clear and useful risk
was later supported by scientists
explanation: The passage says the prediction ‘can never be shown wrong, and that is exactly the weakness’ of it; it fits any outcome and so tells us nothing. It is the opposite of a theory that takes a risk.

stem: Which statement best describes how the author treats Popper's view?
options: The author rejects it as completely mistaken and outdated.
The author accepts every part of it without any reservation.
The author notes criticism but says its core still holds.
The author argues that it applies only to the study of birds.
explanation: The author reports a criticism, that scientists do not drop a theory after one disagreeing result, but then writes ‘Even so, his central idea remains widely taught’. That is neither full rejection nor acceptance without reservation.

title: When grasshoppers swarm
text: The desert locust is a kind of grasshopper that lives in the dry lands stretching from West Africa to India and Pakistan. For most of the time, it leads a quiet, solitary life. Individual locusts are green or brown, avoid one another and do little damage. Everything changes after unusually heavy rains. Plants spring up, the locusts breed rapidly, and when the vegetation dries out again the young insects are forced together on the remaining patches of green. Crowding sets off a remarkable transformation. Repeated touching of their hind legs triggers chemical changes in the locusts' nervous system, and within a few hours they start to seek each other out instead of avoiding one another. Over the following weeks and generations, they change colour to yellow and black, develop stronger flight muscles and begin to move in huge bands and then swarms. A large swarm can contain many millions of insects, travel more than a hundred kilometres in a day with the wind, and eat roughly its own weight in crops and pasture every day. Because swarms cross many borders, control depends on cooperation between countries. Survey teams watch breeding areas after rains, and satellite data on rainfall and vegetation help them predict where outbreaks might begin. Stopping a swarm early, before it grows, is far cheaper and more effective than fighting it once it has spread.

stem: According to the passage, the change in locust behaviour is triggered by
options: a sudden fall in temperature
the colour of the plants they eat
being crowded together closely
winds carrying them across borders
explanation: The passage says ‘Crowding sets off a remarkable transformation’: repeated touching of the hind legs causes chemical changes in the nervous system. Wind is mentioned only for how far a swarm travels once it has formed.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘solitary’ most nearly means
options: living alone
completely silent
rarely seen
very small
explanation: The next sentence explains it: individual locusts ‘avoid one another’, so a solitary locust lives on its own. Nothing in the passage refers to the insects' sound or size.

stem: The last sentence of the passage makes the point that locust control is most successful when
options: it is carried out by one country alone
action is taken early, before swarms grow
swarms are attacked only after they have spread widely
farmers wait for the rains to stop
explanation: The final sentence says stopping a swarm early, before it grows, is far cheaper and more effective than fighting it once it has spread. The passage also says control depends on cooperation between countries, so one country alone is wrong.

title: The Grand Trunk Road
text: For more than two thousand years, travellers, traders and armies have moved along a great route across the north of the subcontinent, linking the plains of Bengal with Lahore, Peshawar and, beyond the Khyber Pass, Kabul. Today it is known as the Grand Trunk Road, and in Pakistan much of its course is followed by the national highway N-5. The road owes much of its shape to Sher Shah Suri, who ruled northern India for a few years in the 1540s. In that short time he had a long stretch of it rebuilt and extended. Along the way he ordered the construction of sarais, roadside inns where travellers could rest and find water and food, at regular intervals. Trees were planted for shade, wells were dug, and tall brick pillars known as kos minars marked distances. Messengers on horseback could change to fresh horses at the sarais, so news travelled far faster than before. Later rulers maintained the road, and in the nineteenth century it was resurfaced and given the name by which it is known today. The road did more than carry goods. Because people of many regions met and mixed along it, it spread languages, foods, crafts and ideas. Writers have often described it as a river of life, and even today a journey along it passes through a long chain of towns that grew up beside it.

stem: According to the passage, the sarais built along the road were
options: tall brick pillars that marked distances
rows of trees planted for shade
wells dug beside the road
roadside inns for travellers to rest
explanation: The passage defines sarais as ‘roadside inns where travellers could rest and find water and food’. The brick pillars that marked distances were the kos minars, a separate feature.

stem: According to the passage, news travelled faster along the road because
options: the road was entirely resurfaced in the nineteenth century
trees gave shade to people walking along it
messengers could change to fresh horses at the sarais
traders carried letters between the towns
explanation: The passage says messengers on horseback could change to fresh horses at the sarais, ‘so news travelled far faster than before’. The resurfacing came about three centuries later and is not linked to the speed of news.

stem: By calling the road ‘a river of life’, writers most likely mean that it
options: carried a constant, varied flow of people and culture
was often flooded by nearby rivers during the rainy season
followed the course of a major river
supplied water to the towns beside it
explanation: The phrase comes right after the passage explains that people of many regions met and mixed along the road, spreading languages, foods, crafts and ideas; like a river, it carried a never-ending flow. Nothing in the passage mentions floods, so the image is not literal.

title: How chess got faster
text: Chess is played today in almost every country, but its earliest known form, called chaturanga, appeared in India around the sixth century. Its pieces represented the four divisions of an ancient army: foot soldiers, horsemen, elephants and chariots, led by a king and his chief adviser. From India the game travelled to Persia, where it was known as shatranj. The Persian phrase shah mat, roughly ‘the king is helpless’, is the source of the English word checkmate. The game was later taken up across the Arab world, where players wrote books analysing positions and composed puzzles, and from there it reached Europe through Spain and Italy around the tenth century. For several hundred years the rules stayed close to the Persian ones, and games were slow. The adviser could move only one square diagonally, and the elephant could jump just two squares, so the pieces took a long time to meet. Then, at the end of the fifteenth century, players in southern Europe made a dramatic change. The adviser became the queen and gained the power to move any distance in any direction, and the elephant's successor could sweep along whole diagonals. Attacks became faster and more dangerous, and the modern game was born. Chess has continued to change in other ways. In 1997 a computer, Deep Blue, defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov in a match, and today almost every serious player trains with chess programs.

stem: According to the passage, the English word ‘checkmate’ comes from
options: the name chaturanga used in India
a Persian phrase about the king
a book of Arab chess puzzles
the name of a European queen
explanation: The passage states that the Persian phrase shah mat, roughly ‘the king is helpless’, is the source of checkmate. Chaturanga is the name of the earliest Indian form of the game, not the origin of this word.

stem: According to the passage, games became faster at the end of the fifteenth century because
options: computers began to analyse positions
the game reached Spain and Italy
elephants and chariots were removed from the board
two pieces were given much greater range
explanation: The adviser became the queen and could move any distance in any direction, and the elephant's successor could sweep whole diagonals, so ‘Attacks became faster’. The game had reached Spain and Italy about five centuries earlier, while games were still slow.

stem: The passage as a whole is mainly concerned with
options: the rules for winning a modern game of chess
how computers came to defeat world champions
how chess spread and changed over the centuries
why chess was first invented to train real armies in India
explanation: The passage traces chess from India to Persia, the Arab world and Europe, then describes the rule change that made the modern game and its later use of computers. Deep Blue is one final example, and the army pieces only describe what chaturanga represented, not why it was invented.

title: Seeing with sound
text: In the 1790s, the Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani carried out a puzzling experiment. Bats that could not see still flew easily around obstacles in a dark room, but bats whose ears were blocked blundered into walls. Spallanzani concluded that bats somehow ‘see’ with their ears, yet he could not explain how, since he heard nothing. The answer came in the late 1930s, when the American researcher Donald Griffin used new equipment that could detect sounds too high for human ears. He found that flying bats give out a rapid series of high-pitched calls and listen for the echoes. He named the method echolocation. An echo carries a great deal of information. The time it takes to return tells the bat how far away an object is, and small differences between the sound reaching its two ears tell it the direction. As a bat closes in on an insect, it calls faster and faster, up to about two hundred times a second, so that it can follow every turn of its prey. Not all bats hunt this way; many large fruit-eating bats rely mainly on their eyes and sense of smell. The insects have not been idle either. Some moths can hear bat calls and drop suddenly towards the ground when one approaches, and a few produce clicks of their own that seem to confuse the hunter.

stem: According to the passage, a bat judges how far away an object is from
options: the time an echo takes to return
the difference between its two ears
the brightness of the object
the smell of the insect
explanation: The passage says the time an echo takes to return tells the bat how far away an object is. Differences between the sound at its two ears tell it the direction, not the distance.

stem: Spallanzani could not explain his results mainly because
options: the bats he tested were unable to fly in the dark
he could not hear the sounds the bats made
he had blocked the ears of every bat
Griffin had already explained them
explanation: The passage says he could not explain how bats ‘see’ with their ears ‘since he heard nothing’; the calls were too high for human ears, which Griffin later showed with new equipment. The blinded bats did fly easily in the dark, so the first option contradicts the passage.

stem: The sentence ‘The insects have not been idle either’ suggests that
options: insects are generally more active than bats at night
moths have stopped flying near bats
bats no longer hunt moths at all
some prey have developed defences against bats
explanation: The sentence introduces moths that hear bat calls and dive, and others that click to confuse the hunter: ways of fighting back against echolocation. ‘Not idle’ refers to these responses, not to how active insects are at night.

title: Inside the Khewra salt mine
text: In the Salt Range of northern Punjab, near the town of Khewra in Jhelum District, lies one of the oldest and largest salt mines in the world. The salt there formed hundreds of millions of years ago, when an ancient sea dried up and left thick beds of minerals that were later buried and pushed upwards by movements of the Earth's crust. Much of Khewra's rock salt is pink or reddish, a colour that comes from small traces of other minerals, especially iron; purer layers are white or clear. Salt has been dug here for many centuries, but the mine's modern layout dates from 1872, when a British mining engineer planned its main tunnels. Khewra is worked by the room-and-pillar method. Miners cut out large chambers but leave about half the salt standing as thick columns that hold up the roof. This wastes a great deal of salt, yet it is far safer than removing everything, because salt can slowly creep and flow under heavy pressure. Galleries run for many kilometres and descend through several levels inside the mountain. Today Khewra is also one of Pakistan's best-known tourist sites. Visitors ride a small train into the mountain to see illuminated chambers, a pool of brine and models built from blocks of salt. The same salt that once went mainly to kitchens and cattle is now sold worldwide in decorative lamps and as coarse pink table salt.

stem: According to the passage, the pink colour of much of Khewra's salt comes from
options: the coloured lights that are placed in the chambers
the brine pool inside the mine
small traces of minerals such as iron
the age of the ancient sea
explanation: The passage says the pink or reddish colour ‘comes from small traces of other minerals, especially iron’, and that purer layers are white or clear. The illuminated chambers are a tourist feature and do not colour the salt itself.

stem: According to the passage, miners at Khewra leave about half the salt in place because
options: the remaining salt is too impure to sell
tourists visiting the mine want to see the original rock
the 1872 plan forbade any further digging
the pillars keep the roof from collapsing
explanation: In the room-and-pillar method the salt is left as ‘thick columns that hold up the roof’, which is safer because salt creeps under heavy pressure. The passage admits this wastes salt, so it is not left because it is impure.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘creep’ most nearly means
options: move quietly to avoid notice
shift gradually over time
grow along the ground
feel a sense of unease
explanation: Salt that can ‘slowly creep and flow under heavy pressure’ changes shape little by little, which is why pillars are needed. Moving quietly to avoid notice is how a person creeps, a sense that does not fit rock.

title: Fighting noise with noise
text: On a long bus journey or a flight, the steady roar of an engine can be tiring even when it is not especially loud. Noise-cancelling headphones reduce such sound by adding more sound. The idea depends on the fact that sound is a wave of tiny pressure changes in the air. When two waves meet, they combine. If the high-pressure part of one wave arrives at the same moment as the low-pressure part of another wave of the same size, the two cancel out and the result is near silence. This effect is called destructive interference. In noise-cancelling headphones, small microphones on the outside of each ear cup pick up the surrounding noise. Electronic circuits then produce a matching wave that is exactly reversed, sometimes called anti-noise, and the headphone speaker plays it together with the music. The approach works best on steady, low-pitched sounds such as the hum of an engine or an air conditioner, because these change slowly and are easy to predict. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, such as a baby crying or people talking nearby, change too quickly to be cancelled fully; for these, the headphones rely mostly on the cushions that seal around the ears and block sound in the ordinary way. The basic principle was patented in the 1930s, but it became practical only with small, fast electronics, and it was first widely used in headsets for pilots.

stem: According to the passage, noise-cancelling headphones reduce steady noise mainly by
options: playing a reversed copy of the noise
making the music much louder
sealing the ears completely with thick cushions
filtering the air around the ears
explanation: Microphones pick up the noise and circuits produce ‘a matching wave that is exactly reversed’, which the speaker plays so that the waves cancel. The cushions matter mainly for sudden or high-pitched sounds, not for the steady noise the method targets.

stem: As used in the passage, the word ‘steady’ most nearly means
options: firmly fixed in one place
calm and sensible
constant and unchanging
slow and careful
explanation: Steady sounds such as an engine's hum are described as ones that ‘change slowly and are easy to predict’, so steady means constant. ‘Firmly fixed in one place’ is the sense used for a ladder or a table, not for a sound.

stem: Based on the passage, which of the following would noise-cancelling headphones most likely cancel least effectively?
options: the hum of a refrigerator
the drone of an aircraft engine
the whirr of an air conditioner
the sudden bark of a dog
explanation: The passage says sudden or high-pitched sounds change too quickly to be cancelled fully, while steady, low-pitched hums are cancelled best. A dog's sudden bark is the only sudden sound listed; the other three are steady hums like the engine and air conditioner in the passage.
